I agree with the group that A is the unassailable textbook example and we should start there.

Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and OSA s.103(1)(a) / NI 45-106 s.2.34 makes a bond, debenture, note or other evidence of indebtedness issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act Canada applies an exempt security / exempt distribution. The exemption is issuer and security based, retail neutral and purchaser financial condition is immaterial. A non-prospectus distribution of the bank’s own bonds to retail investors in Ontario is the classic bank-debt exempt distribution. B, C and D are correctly disposed of on that basis: B is not a Bank Act Canada bank, C fails accredited / minimum amount / family friends / business associates and D is the bank equity trap – s.103(1)(a) is debt only.

The fact pattern that is doing the real work in this set is E and that is why the zero net assets / unemployed purchaser detail is pleaded there and not in A.

OSA s.103(1)(b) and NI 45-106 s.2.18 provide an issuer based prospectus exemption for securities of a credit union, caisse populaire or co-operative credit association. It is not an accredited investor test and it is not conditioned on net assets, income or employment status. That is the co-operative analogue of the bank-debt exemption in A.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisse populaire constituted under New Brunswick credit union legislation. NI 45-106 s.2.18 is framed by reference to credit unions and caisses populaires registered under provincial credit union legislation, not only to a federally constituted entity under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. Ontario practice treats a provincially registered caisse populaire as falling within the s.103(1)(b)/s.2.18 issuer based exemption. The inclusion of a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed is not a defect, it is the point: the exemption is designed to operate precisely where the purchaser is unaccredited and would otherwise be unable to participate.

The “member only / federal constitution” objection conflates the federal securities concepts with the NI 45-106 credit union exemption which expressly captures credit unions and caisses populaires registered under provincial law. On the conventional Ontario teaching formulation the distribution of shares of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée without a prospectus is prospectus exempt and the purchaser’s financial condition is immaterial in exactly the same retail neutral way it is immaterial for the bank-debt exemption in A.

So the uncontroversial compliant example is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution, and the textbook co-operative counterpart on the stated facts is E. If the question is being used to test the non-obvious issuer based retail neutral exemption – which is what the zero net asset / unemployed purchaser fact is signalling – the intended illustration is E, the credit union / caisses populaires share distribution, with A as the obvious bank-debt anchor.

On the framework we are all using – OSA s.53 displaced only by an OSA s.103 / NI 45-106 exemption in force in January 2020 – the issuer / security based exemptions are determinative here.

Bank debt, debt only, issuer / security based

OSA s.103(1)(a) / NI 45-106 s.2.34 makes a bond, debenture, note or other evidence of indebtedness issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act Canada applies, Schedules I/II/III, an exempt security / exempt distribution. The exemption is retail neutral and purchaser financial condition is immaterial.

* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act Canada bank and the securities are its own bonds. A non-prospectus distribution of its own debt to retail investors in Ontario is the classic bank-debt exempt distribution. A is compliant.
* B. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent, not a bank to which the Bank Act Canada applies and not a Schedule I/II/III Bank Act Canadian bank. No accredited investor / eligible investor / $150k Ontario minimum amount investment / OM / family friends business associates reliance is pleaded for a broad public like distribution. Non-compliant.
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. s.103(1)(a) / s.2.34 is debt only. Bank equity is not listed. The large retail pool including a zero net asset unemployed purchaser is the bank-equity trap. No investor based exemption is made out. Non-compliant.

Investor based / private issuer

Accredited individual NI 45-106 s.1.1 Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k/$300k with spouse; Ontario minimum amount investment = $150k.

* C. Private issuer shares to an unconnected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. No accredited status, no family/friends/business associates connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM facts. Prospectus required. Non-compliant.

Credit union / caisses populaires

OSA s.103(1)(b) and NI 45-106 s.2.18 provide an issuer based exemption for securities of a credit union / caisse populaire / co-operative credit association. On the conventional Ontario teaching reading the exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on accredited status, net assets or income. The purchaser’s financial condition is immaterial, exactly as it is immaterial for the bank-debt exemption in A.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a caisse populaire / co-operative credit association constituted under provincial credit union legislation. NI 45-106 s.2.18 is framed by reference to provincial credit union / caisse populaire legislation. The distribution of its membership shares without a prospectus is the co-operative analogue of A. The fact that the offering is to a large number of retail investors including a purchaser with $0 net assets who is unemployed is the illustration of the issuer based retail neutral nature of the exemption, not a defect.

On that conventional issuer based reading the compliant distributions on the pleaded facts are A, the Canadian bank-debt distribution, and E, the credit-union / caisses populaires share distribution. B, C and D are prospectus required on the stated facts.

The strict statutory / member-only / federal Co-operative Credit Associations Act caveat is noted. On a strict reading that limits s.103(1)(b)/s.2.18 to a federally constituted co-operative credit association and/or to a member-only distribution, a broad public retail offer by a provincial New Brunswick caisse in Ontario would fall outside the exemption and the only unqualified compliant distribution on the facts as pleaded would be A. I’m with everyone on the bank-debt anchor.

OSA s.103(1)(a)/NI 45-106 s.2.34 is issuer/security based and retail neutral. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds issued by the bank itself. A non-prospectus distribution of the bank’s own debt to retail investors in Ontario is the classic textbook example and purchaser financial condition is immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant.

C is investor based and fails: private issuer shares to an unconnected purchaser with salary $35k and net assets $10k, no accredited status, no FFBA connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM. D is the bank-equity trap: s.103(1)(a)/s.2.34 is debt only, Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares, and there is no accredited/minimum amount/OM/FFBA reliance made out.

The exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on accredited status, net assets, income or employment.

NI 45-106 s.2.18 is framed by reference to provincial credit union/caisse populaire legislation and Ontario practice treats a provincially registered caisse populaire as falling within s.103(1)(b)/s.2.18. The offering is to a large number of retail investors and one of them is pleaded as having zero dollars of net assets and being unemployed.
